Chapter 2: The Dual Control Model—How Brakes and Accelerators Shape Desire
Now that we've got a handle on sexual diversity, let's dive deeper into something called the dual control model.
This isn't just a clever metaphor—it's actually a practical way to understand how desire and arousal work in real life.
Picture your sexual system like a car. You've got an accelerator, which gets pressed by things that feel exciting, safe, or just plain sexy. And then there's the brake, which reacts to anything that signals discomfort, distraction, or even a tiny sense of threat.
Both pedals are always in play, and it's that balance between them that decides whether your “car” moves forward—or just stays put.
For a lot of women, the brake is actually more sensitive than the accelerator. So, you might have plenty of turn-ons in the mix, but just one strong turn-off can slam everything to a halt. Think about it—stress, worries about your body, a tense relationship, or even just a cluttered bedroom can all act as brakes.
On the flip side, feeling safe, relaxed, and really connected can let up on the brake, giving your accelerator some room to work its magic.
Let’s break this down a little more. What are some common accelerators?
Well, feeling desired or attractive. Positive touch—a hug, a gentle caress. Erotic cues like a certain look, sound, or scent. And of course, that sense of emotional intimacy and trust.
Now, what hits the brakes?
Stress or anxiety. Feeling self-conscious about your body. Fears of being judged or rejected. And, honestly, even simple distractions in your environment.
Here’s something to pay attention to: understanding your own unique mix of accelerators and brakes is a total game changer.
It’s not just about adding more turn-ons. Sometimes, figuring out what’s pressing your brakes—and easing up on those—can make all the difference.
Picture someone who’s had a long, stressful day and just doesn’t feel any desire. The real issue might not be attraction at all—it’s just that the brake is jammed down by stress and exhaustion. So, what if you focused on lowering your stress or making your space more relaxing? That could be the key to reigniting desire.
The dual control model also helps explain why desire can shift over time. Big life changes—a new job, becoming a parent, dealing with health stuff—these can all tweak the balance between accelerator and brake.
And the important thing? That’s normal. It’s not a failure or something to be ashamed of. It’s just part of being human.
So, what can you actually do with this knowledge? Here are a few practical steps:
First, take a little time to think back on your own experiences. What tends to hit your accelerator? And what usually presses your brakes?
Then, share these insights with your partner. It opens up understanding, support, and closeness.
And finally, remember—it’s just as important to reduce the brakes as it is to try and add more accelerators.
When you take this approach, you move away from trying to “fix” desire, and instead, you start to understand and work with the natural ebb and flow of your own sexual response.
It invites curiosity, a spirit of experimentation, and a lot more kindness—both for yourself and your partner.
